children: The Reserve Bank of India’s reported rejection of Tata Sons’ application to surrender its non-banking finance company registration could make it easier for the Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group to refinance its expensive Rs 21,500-crore debt at a lower cost, as it substantially improves the prospects of an eventual listing of the Tata Group holding company, people aware of the matter told
Moneycontrol.

Improved visibility on Tata Sons listing will provide a clearer route for the SP Group to monetise part of its 18.4 percent stake in Tata Sons, against which it has raised large amounts of debt. The development is expected to strengthen the group’s position when it seeks to refinance the high-cost private credit raised in July, the people said.

The development could also provide more immediate breathing room. Lenders may consider rolling over a Rs 3,500-crore repayment due by the end of September or grant the group a waiver from meeting the deadline, now that a Tata Sons listing appears more likely, the people said.
Expensive refinancing

Finding a route to monetise its Tata Sons stake has become increasingly important for the SP Group after it completed the Rs 21,500-crore refinancing in July this year, one of the largest private-credit transactions involving an Indian corporate group. The deal addressed immediate funding requirements but left the group carrying expensive debt.

The refinancing comprised about Rs 15,200 crore of three-year, rupee-denominated zero-coupon bonds issued by Eqyizen Investment at a yield of 18.95 percent and a $650-million bond issued by Mercury Finance at a yield of 14.5 percent. Both were raised largely against the group’s Tata Sons holding.
The financing carries a ‘make-whole’ provision for around 18 months, making an early refinancing expensive,
Moneycontrol
reported on August 28. Such a clause requires the borrower to compensate lenders for some of the interest they would lose if the debt is repaid ahead of schedule.

The make-whole protection is expected to expire around June 2027, after which the SP Group could seek to refinance the debt at a substantially lower cost. It is looking to bring borrowing costs down from around 18–19 percent currently to closer to 12 percent through a future refinancing,
Moneycontrol
had reported.

Lenders had previously indicated that another refinancing, or further relaxation of loan-to-value requirements, would be difficult unless the group demonstrated tangible progress towards monetising its Tata Sons stake. The RBI decision improves visibility on one of the clearest potential exit routes, although an actual listing and subsequent stake sale could still take time.
Immediate repayment pressure
Moneycontrol

reported on August 27 that the SP Group was required to pay around Rs 3,500 crore to holders of instruments from an earlier financing by the end of September. The payment was to be made from the July refinancing proceeds, but part of the money was retained by the group for its own requirements.

Failure to meet the deadline could be construed as an event of default under the financing terms, people familiar with the matter had said. Completing the payment would also reduce the loan-to-value ratio on lenders’ exposure to around 32 percent from about 40 percent.
The increased likelihood of a liquidity event could, however, make lenders more willing to give the group additional time, sources said.
RBI rejects deregistration

The RBI has rejected Tata Sons’ request to voluntarily surrender its certificate of registration as a core investment company, CNBC-TV18 reported on September 12. The decision closes the principal regulatory route Tata Sons had pursued to remain unlisted after repaying its borrowings and applying for deregistration.

Tata Sons was identified as an upper-layer NBFC in September 2022. Under the RBI’s scale-based regulatory framework, an unlisted upper-layer NBFC must list within three years of its identification. That deadline expired in September 2025, but Tata Sons’ deregistration application had remained under consideration.

The rejection makes the listing requirement applicable to Tata Sons, although the timing and contours of any initial public offering remain unclear. It is still too early to determine when the company will begin a formal process, sources said.
However, Tata Sons has spent the past year consolidating and simplifying parts of its subsidiary structure, leaving it better prepared for a situation in which it had to list, the sources added.

The Mistry family, which owns around 18.4 percent of Tata Sons through two entities, is the holding company’s largest minority shareholder. Tata Trusts owns about 66 percent and the rest is owned by Tata Group companies and individual shareholders. The SP Group has repeatedly borrowed against its Tata Sons holding, making a credible monetisation path central to reducing its promoter-level debt.
The latest bond structure also contains milestones linked to the stake. A sales note reviewed earlier by
Moneycontrol
required a resolution, heads of terms for a transaction or an IPO announcement involving Tata Sons within 18 months of issuance. It also called for repayment of Rs 11,275 crore within 24 months.
Queries sent to Tata Sons and the SP Group did not elicit an immediate response.

title: Tata Sons listing prospects may pave way for cheaper refinancing of SP Group’s Rs 21,500 cr promoter debt
